title: Mega backdoor Roth (if your 401(k) supports it)
summary: After-tax 401(k) contributions converted in-service or in-plan to Roth. Up to ~$47,500 of additional tax-free growth space annually in 2026.
detailsHtml:
How it works

The total 2026 401(k) contribution limit (employee + employer + after-tax) is $72,000, or $80,000 with the standard 50+ catch-up, or $83,250 for ages 60–63 with the super catch-up. Your employee deferral takes $24,500; your employer match takes a variable amount; what's left can potentially be filled with after-tax contributions, then converted to Roth — either through an in-service distribution or an in-plan Roth conversion. Once in Roth, the funds grow tax-free.

Example: $200K salary, 5% employer match Employee deferral: $24,500 Employer match: $10,000 Total contribution cap: $72,000 After-tax space: $37,500 → Convert to Roth, grow tax-free

Requirements

Your 401(k) plan must allow both after-tax contributions and either in-service distributions or in-plan Roth conversions. Roughly 30–40% of large employer plans support this; many smaller plans don't. Check your plan document — this is typically not advertised by HR.

The ACP testing constraint most articles miss: After-tax contributions are subject to ACP (Actual Contribution Percentage) nondiscrimination testing. Even when the plan document permits Mega Backdoor Roth, HCEs are often capped well below the §415(c) headroom because the plan would fail ACP otherwise. The practical effect: in a non-Safe Harbor plan, HCEs frequently have $5K–$15K of usable after-tax space, not the headline ~$37K. Safe Harbor 401(k) plans bypass ADP testing but still need a Safe Harbor ACP feature to bypass ACP. Ask your plan administrator about historical HCE after-tax limits before counting on the full space.
Each in-plan Roth conversion starts its own 5-year clock under IRC §408A(d)(2)(B) for the 10% early withdrawal penalty on converted amounts. A 50-year-old converting after-tax to Roth in 2026 cannot withdraw those converted dollars penalty-free until 2031, even after reaching 59½.
Notice 2014-54 ordering — earnings on after-tax contributions are ordinary-income taxable at conversion. IRS Notice 2014-54 governs the bifurcation of after-tax contributions from earnings on those contributions during an in-service distribution or in-plan Roth conversion. The contribution basis converts tax-free; the earnings portion is fully taxable in the conversion year at ordinary rates. If after-tax contributions accumulate for even a month or two before being swept to Roth, meaningful earnings accrue — and those earnings hit at the participant's marginal rate, often 32–37% federal plus NIIT and state. The fix is same-payroll or daily automatic in-plan Roth conversion, which most modern plan documents either permit or don't. Quarterly or annual manual conversion leaks 3–4 figures per year in unnecessary ordinary-income tax for participants filling the full after-tax window. Confirm the plan administrator supports automated conversion before designing the strategy around the full §415(c) headroom.
